# The canonical register: Danu

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Danu, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Danu to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The tradition's record preserves this name in its romanized scholarly form: **Danu** — no older script survives to transcribe, so the canonical content is the exactness of the spelling itself.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: “DAH-noo” The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *danu* differs from the canonical *Danu* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Danu is the Celtic branch of the Indo-European river-mother — kin to the Vedic Danu, mother of the demon Vṛtra in the Rigveda’s oldest combat, across the very language-family the names share.  The Tuatha Dé Danann were euhemerized by the medieval Irish scholars into a people of sorcerers; the modern Celtic revival restored them to goddess-worship, with Danu as the primordial name.

And it never stopped working. Her name survives in the Tuatha Dé Danann’s — the divine race of every Irish legend of consequence — and in the river-network of Europe, the Danube most of all.  The modern Druidic and Celtic-revival movements take Danu as the mother-goddess of their pantheon; and the sídhe-tradition she eponymizes is the ancestor of the world’s entire fairy-canon.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: the tradition’s own standard. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Danu** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Danu** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *danu* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Danu** stands at [/danu/](/danu/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 4 cited sources — Lebor Gabála Érenn (the Book of Invasions), Cath Maige Tuired (the Battles of Mag Tuired), Proto-Celtic *dānu river-name studies (Mallory & Adams).
